title: How this book was made
---

This book was extracted from  


Nothing in this book is typed in by hand. Every game, move and note comes out
of a scan of the printed page by one chain of programs, and that chain is rerun
from the scan on every build. What a person contributed is recorded separately,
in the open, and named below.

## The sources

| Scan | Edition | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `philidor2.txt` | *Analysis of the Game of Chess*, London, P. Elmsley, 1777 | **Base text.** The cleaner scan and the fuller book: it alone carries the endgames and the seventeen rules. |
| `philidor1.txt` | *Analysis of the Game of Chess*, London, 1790, volume I | **Collation only.** It ends "END OF THE FIRST VOLUME", so it covers the parties and gambits and not the endgames. |

Both are public-domain scans of Harvard copies. The PDFs are about 150 MB and
are not kept with the code; the text layer extracted from them is, and is all
the programs ever read. A third edition, the 1819 Kenny translation down the
French line, is read by its owner from a physical copy and enters only as
reported comparisons. [The editions](editions.qmd) sets out how the two lines of
descent relate.

## The chain

It runs one way, out of a single input. No output is ever parsed back in.

```
philidor2.txt   the 1777 scan
     |
     +-- build.py -------> philidor.md      the transcription
     |                     md/*.md          the same text, one game per file
     |
     +-- games.py ------->  games.json      + the algebraic replay
                              |
                              +-- to_pgn.py -----> pgn/*.pgn
                              +-- build_book.py -> book/games/*.qmd -> _site/
```

`philidor.md` and `md/*.md` are written from the same parse, and `games.json`
is emitted by the same single pass over the scan. That is a stronger guarantee
than re-reading Markdown would give: there is no second parser that could
disagree with the first, and every line keeps the number of the source line it
came from, so any editorial decision can be checked against the page.

## Extraction

**Normalise the scan.** The long *s* becomes *s*, and so do the scanner's
misreadings of it as *f*: `fame` → same, `fide` → side, `loft` → lost. That
list was not guessed. Every word containing an *f* was tested against a
dictionary, keeping those where the substitution produced a real word the
original was not, and the result was then read by eye. The same pass repairs
Cyrillic and Greek homoglyphs, rejoins words the scan broke or ran together,
and drops running heads, page numbers and printers' marks.

**Find the games.** A table of 96 sections, each keyed to its line in the scan,
drives the split. Eight were missed on the first pass because the scanner had
set their headings in Cyrillic lookalikes — `ВАСK-GAME` reads as Latin but is
not — or split them mid-word. They surfaced through the notes: Philidor letters
them a…i, k…u, w, x, y, the eighteenth-century sequence that omits *j* and *v*,
and that sequence restarts only at a heading.

**Separate moves from notes.** The word NOTES is printed as a centred rule and
the scan shatters it across up to three lines, so it cannot be matched. The
parser keys off the note bodies instead: a line opening `(a)` starts the notes,
and the next move number ends them.

**Rebuild the numbering.** The printed move numbers are unreliable — `37-`,
`3:`, `II.`, `ΙΙ.` — so plies are paired into moves from scratch, and the
result is *checked against* what the printer set rather than taken from it.

Spelling is otherwise the translator's: "shews" and "chuse" stand as he had
them. Corrections to the printed text are held in an `ERRATA` table keyed by
line number, two entries at present, each quoting the source line as it stands
and saying what settled it. Where the source is defective beyond repair, the
transcription says so instead of quietly patching it.

## Descriptive to algebraic: constrain, don't translate

No move is ever computed. Each ply is parsed for what it *does* say, the board
is asked for every legal move that fits, and the rules of chess eliminate the
rest. Descriptive notation is ambiguous as language; a position rarely is.

- **The piece** is the last noun of the possessive chain. In "the queen's
  bishop's pawn" it is the pawn; everything before it names the file it started
  on. Reading that phrase as a bishop was the first bug.
- **The square** takes its file from the last qualifier before the ordinal, and
  at a tie the longest. The rank counts from the owner's back rank, and
  "adverse" flips which side you count from.
- **A bare qualifier** inherits its wing from the piece moving: "the queen, at
  her bishop's second square" means the queen's bishop, not the king's.
- **Special forms**: captures, pawn pushes by distance and file, castling,
  "covers the check", "gives check" with no square named, and "the same", which
  mirrors the opponent's previous move.

Where a ply still admits several readings, each is tried and whichever lets the
rest of the game replay legally is kept, depth-first with a node cap. Two
structural transforms sit on top: the four games set out *beginning with the
Black* replay with the colours exchanged, and a back-game is a variation rather
than a game, so its parent's plies are prepended up to the branch move.

The endgames state their opening position in the same descriptive notation as
the moves — "The king, at his fourth square" — so the same parser reads them.
Twenty-nine studies get a stated position that way, all but one of them read
from the text alone.

## What the search actually decides

Every accepted ply is labelled, and the tally is recomputed on each build.

| How the ply was settled | Plies | Share | What it rests on |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Forced by the position | 3138 | 93.7% | The words and the board leave exactly one legal move. Nothing was chosen. |
| "The same" | 104 | 3.1% | Mirrors the previous move, and the mirror is legal. |
| Chosen by the search | 84 | 2.5% | Several readings fit equally well; the one kept is the one under which the game finishes. |
| Read against the text | 23 | 0.7% | No legal move fits the words. The reading departs from the page and is flagged. |

So the search decides 3.2% of the book, and the other 96.8% is arithmetic. That
cuts both ways: the conversion is mostly not a search result, and where it *is*
a search result is exactly where a reader should look first. Those 84 choice
points are not isolated, either. Replaying greedily, first reading each time and
no backtracking, reaches 2721 of the 3349 plies and dies in 27 games, so
backtracking is what settles 628 plies, and at 48 of them greedy plays a
different move altogether. A handful of decisions gate a fifth of the book.

## Cross-comparison

Legality alone would be a poor judge, so the reading is held against sources
and constraints that do not use it. None of these can be satisfied by the same
mistake that produced the reading.

| Check | Scope | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The four published forms agree — transcription, per-game files, records, book | every move and note | no move or note may go missing or unreachable |
| The printer's own move numbers | 1462 moves | 7 drift, all in numbers the scan mangled |
| Collation against the 1790 edition | the parties and gambits | 60–83% where that scan is legible |
| A back-game meets its parent at the branch move | 49 branches | 49 agree |
| A move does what its own sentence claims | 20094 claims | 4 contradict |
| An independent transcription of 5 lines | 160 plies | 159 identical |
| Positions supplied by hand must be legal and reachable | 3 positions | 2 match the parser, 1 matches a position the game reaches |

The 1790 collation reduces each game to a canonical token sequence, so the
1777 spelled-out text ("The king's pawn, two moves") can be compared with the
1790 abbreviation ("The K. P. two moves"); the ceiling on agreement is that
scan's quality, not a disagreement between the editions. The branch audit is
the strongest check here, because it needs no outside source at all, and it
found the bare-qualifier bug that neither the replay nor the outside
transcription had caught.

The independent transcription is eight of Philidor's games in algebraic
notation posted to a chess.com thread, matched by their moves rather than their
labels. Its one disagreement is real: at Black's 4th move of one party, 1777
reads "the queen's pawn, one move" (d6) where 1790 reads "two moves" (d5), and
the outside line agrees with 1790. Both readings are legal, so nothing in this
machinery could have found it.

**Chapters 70 to 98 have never been read against a second edition**, because
the 1790 file is volume I and the endgames were in volume II.

## Where a person came in

Four kinds of contribution could not come from the scan, and each is recorded
rather than absorbed.

- **Starting positions, supplied as FEN.** Four studies had no working board
  and the maintainer supplied a position for each by hand. Only one was
  genuinely missing; two were already built but a piece short, because a stated
  position can run two pieces onto one line divided by nothing but a comma, and
  the supplied board is what sent the search for that bug. The fourth needed no
  position at all. Three of the four are now kept as a standing check instead
  of a patch. Asking for FEN is what made this safe: three arrived with a `Q`
  where a `K` was meant, so they had no kings, and were rejected loudly at once
  rather than played on quietly.
- **A reader looking at the rendered board.** Two studies were built on the
  wrong squares and replayed perfectly well from them, because the moves that
  follow are legal either way. No audit here could catch that. It was caught by
  the maintainer seeing that the queen stood on the wrong side of the board.
- **A second edition read by hand.** The 1819 confirmed one corrected position
  and disputed one verdict, from a board both editions agree on. Its open
  questions are kept in the repository's `TODO.md`.
- **Editorial readings, in the open.** Where the printed move is destroyed or
  impossible and no rule can recover it, a move can be settled by hand with a
  reason resting on evidence in the book. Anything settled that way is marked
  in the records, tagged in the PGN, stated on the chapter and marked 🐞 in the
  contents. It is never folded silently into what Philidor wrote.

The rule that separates a fix from an exception: when the text is right and the
board plays the wrong move, the converter misread a phrase it should have
understood, so the repair belongs in the parser as a rule. Nearly every stop
found so far has been of that kind, and a fix that reads one game further while
breaking another is not a fix — the audits say so.

## What this method cannot do

- **Legality is a filter, not an oracle.** Where two readings are both legal
  the search has nothing to separate them and will not notice. The d6/d5
  misprint is exactly that case.
- **A complete replay is not proof.** A wrong board played 27 plies quite
  happily before the claims check caught it. Finishing means only that some
  legal reading exists, not that it is Philidor's.
- **The first complete replay wins.** The search stops at the first success, so
  where a game completes, that reading is not known to be the only one.
- **Failure is not proof either.** The budget and node caps mean a game can
  stop for want of search rather than for want of a reading. The unconverted
  plies are "not found", not "not there".
- **The headline double-counts.** Of the 3349 converted plies, 757 are a
  back-game replaying its parent, so only 2592 are distinct positions read from
  the page.

A reading can be lawful from beginning to end and still be wrong. Only
redundancy catches that: a second edition, an outside transcription, the
branch-point positions, Philidor's own notes, and a person looking at the
board. [State of the conversion](state.qmd) says where each game stands today.

## A note on the rules

Philidor judges his endgames under the seventeen rules the 1777 edition closes
with, and they are not the modern laws: a stalemated player **won** the game in
England, promotion had been restricted to a captured piece in the 1749 edition,
and the fifty-move rule was claimed rather than automatic. The boards here play
modern chess, which is what `python-chess` enforces, so where Philidor calls a
position won or drawn he may be reasoning under a different code. It matters
most in the endgames.
